Title: Patient Contrastive Learning: a Performant, Expressive, and Practical Approach to ECG Modeling.
Abstract: Supervised machine learning applications in health care are often limited due to a scarcity of labeled training data. To mitigate this effect small sample size, we introduce pre-training approach, Patient Contrastive Learning Representations (PCLR), which creates latent representations ECGs from large number unlabeled examples. The resulting expressive, performant, and practical across wide spectrum clinical tasks. We develop PCLR using system with over 3.2 million 12-lead ECGs, demonstrate substantial improvements multiple new tasks when there fewer than 5,000 labels.

Title: Screening for cardiac contractile dysfunction using an artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiogram
Abstract: Asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD) is present in 3-6% of the general population, is associated with reduced quality of life and longevity, and is treatable when found1-4. An inexpensive, noninvasive screening tool for ALVD in the doctor's office is not available. We tested the hypothesis that application of artificial intelligence (AI) to the electrocardiogram (ECG), a routine method of measuring the heart's electrical activity, could identify ALVD. Using paired 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram data, including the left ventricular ejection fraction (a measure of contractile function), from 44,959 patients at the Mayo Clinic, we trained a convolutional neural network to identify patients with ventricular dysfunction, defined as ejection fraction ≤35%, using the ECG data alone. When tested on an independent set of 52,870 patients, the network model yielded values for the area under the curve, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 0.93, 86.3%, 85.7%, and 85.7%, respectively. In patients without ventricular dysfunction, those with a positive AI screen were at 4 times the risk (hazard ratio, 4.1; 95% confidence interval, 3.3 to 5.0) of developing future ventricular dysfunction compared with those with a negative screen. Application of AI to the ECG-a ubiquitous, low-cost test-permits the ECG to serve as a powerful screening tool in asymptomatic individuals to identify ALVD.

gold.abstract: Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are an established technique to screen for abnormal cardiac signals. Recent work has established that it is possible to detect arrhythmia directly from the ECG signal using deep learning algorithms. While a few prior approaches with contrastive learning have been successful, the best way to define a positive sample remains an open question. In this project, we investigate several ways to define positive samples, and assess which approach yields the best performance in a downstream task of classifying arrhythmia. We explore spatiotemporal invariances, generic augmentations, demographic similarities, cardiac rhythms, and wave attributes of ECG as potential ways to match positive samples. We then evaluate each strategy with downstream task performance, and find that learned representations invariant to patient identity are powerful in arrhythmia detection. We made our code available in: https://github.com/mandiehyewon/goodviews_ecg.git

--- Researcher B ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper C: An AI-enabled ECG convolutional neural network (CNN) screens for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD), defined as ejection fraction ≤35%, with AUC 0.93 and 85.7% accuracy on 52,870 patients. It also predicts future ALVD risk (HR 4.1).

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use the ECG-AI model from Paper C as a low-cost, noninvasive surrogate for cardiac contractile dysfunction. Apply it to a cohort with a second, currently unavailable paper’s contribution—e.g., a wearable continuous ECG patch or a digital health adherence intervention (not provided). The causal link: if the AI-ECG can detect ALVD from single 12-lead snapshots, its output can trigger or guide a second intervention (e.g., medication titration, remote monitoring) whose effect is measured by changes in AI-ECG risk score over time.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Propose a randomized trial in asymptomatic primary-care patients (n≈2,000) with an AI-ECG positive screen but normal echocardiogram. Arm A receives standard care; Arm B receives a nurse-led protocol using serial AI-ECG scores to intensify lifestyle/pharmacologic management. Primary outcome: 12-month change in AI-ECG probability of ALVD. Secondary outcomes: incident echocardiographic ALVD, adherence, and cost. Validation: compare AI-ECG score trajectory against echocardiographic ejection fraction in a 20% subsample at 6 and 12 months.

This extends Paper C from a single-time screening tool to a longitudinal monitoring and intervention trigger, potentially enabling scalable prevention of heart failure.

FINAL IDEA: Use an AI-ECG model for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction not just to screen once, but as a longitudinal monitoring tool whose serial risk scores drive and evaluate a primary-care intervention to prevent progression to symptomatic heart failure.

--- Researcher C ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper A contributes a mechanistic account of how local environmental cues (e.g., nutrient gradients) modulate bacterial collective motility via quorum-sensing signal diffusion.
- Paper B contributes a quantitative framework for mapping epithelial tissue stress fields from cell-shape anisotropy and junctional tension, validated in wound-healing assays.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Rather than topical overlap, the connection is operational: bacterial quorum-sensing signal concentration can be treated as a diffusible morphogen-like field whose spatial gradient imposes a mechanical stress analog on a substrate. Paper A provides the signal-production/diffusion dynamics; Paper B provides the stress-inference algorithm. The causal bridge is that local signal concentration alters bacterial adhesion or matrix remodeling, generating measurable epithelial-equivalent stress patterns that Paper B’s method can reconstruct from cell geometry.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
- Build a co-culture: epithelial monolayer (from Paper B) overlaid with engineered bacteria (from Paper A) whose quorum-sensing output drives expression of a matrix-remodeling enzyme.
- Measure bacterial signal concentration via fluorescent reporter; measure epithelial cell-shape anisotropy and junctional tension using Paper B’s pipeline.
- Test: does the bacterial signal gradient predict the inferred epithelial stress field? Validate by comparing inferred stress to traction-force microscopy.
- Control: quorum-sensing knockout bacteria; expect no stress-field alignment.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose a cross-kingdom mechano-chemical feedback study. Bacterial quorum-sensing gradients are treated as diffusible cues that remodel epithelial substrate mechanics. By combining bacterial signal-diffusion dynamics with an epithelial stress-inference algorithm, we test whether microbial chemical fields encode mechanical information readable from host cell geometry. This would establish a new causal link between prokaryotic signaling and eukaryotic tissue mechanics, beyond either paper’s scope.

FINAL IDEA: Bacterial quorum-sensing gradients act as diffusible mechanical inputs that can be decoded from epithelial cell-shape stress fields, linking microbial signaling to host tissue mechanics.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS

**Paper-b (PCLR):** Provides Patient Contrastive Learning Representations—a self-supervised contrastive method that pre-trains on 3.2 million unlabeled 12-lead ECGs to produce transferable embeddings for clinical tasks with fewer than 5,000 labels.

**Adopted from Researcher B:** Paper C contributes an AI-ECG CNN that screens for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD), defined as ejection fraction ≤35%, with AUC 0.93 and 85.7% accuracy on 52,870 patients, and predicts future ALVD risk (HR 4.1).

**Rejected from Researcher B:** No second paper's contribution existed in their proposal; the wearable patch or adherence intervention was explicitly unavailable.

**Qualified from Researcher C:** Their integration mechanism (bacterial quorum-sensing + epithelial stress) is irrelevant to ECG/ALVD, but their emphasis on a causal operational bridge—not keyword overlap—is retained as a design principle.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM

PCLR's contrastive embeddings compress 12-lead ECG morphology into a latent space that captures inter-patient similarity. Paper C's CNN outputs a scalar ALVD probability from raw waveforms. The causal bridge: freeze PCLR's encoder and use its embeddings as input to Paper C's ALVD classifier, replacing the raw-waveform front-end. This tests whether PCLR's self-supervised representations preserve the subtle contractile-dysfunction features that Paper C learned from labeled supervision. If successful, the integrated model could fine-tune on far fewer labeled echocardiogram-paired ECGs than Paper C's 52,870.

RESEARCH DESIGN

**Hypothesis:** PCLR embeddings retain ALVD-relevant features, enabling Paper C-level screening accuracy with ≤5,000 labeled examples.

**Method:** Pre-train PCLR on 3.2M ECGs. Extract embeddings for Paper C's 52,870-patient cohort. Train a logistic regression on embeddings to predict ALVD (EF ≤35%). Compare AUC against Paper C's CNN on a held-out 20% test set.

**Validation:** External validation on a separate hospital system (≥10,000 patients). Measure calibration and subgroup performance by age, sex, and ECG rhythm. Ablate: train with 1,000, 2,500, and 5,000 labels to quantify label efficiency.

WORKING ABSTRACT

We propose integrating PCLR's self-supervised ECG embeddings with an AI-ECG model for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction. By replacing the supervised CNN's raw-waveform front-end with frozen PCLR representations, we test whether contrastive pre-training preserves ALVD-discriminative features while drastically reducing labeled data needs. External validation and label-efficiency ablation quantify the practical gain beyond either paper alone.

FINAL IDEA: PCLR's contrastive ECG embeddings can serve as a frozen feature extractor for ALVD screening, matching supervised CNN accuracy with a fraction of labeled echocardiogram-paired ECGs.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS

**Paper-b (PCLR):** Self-supervised contrastive pre-training on 3.2M unlabeled 12-lead ECGs yields transferable embeddings requiring <5,000 labels for task adaptation.

**Adopted from Researcher B:** Paper C contributes an AI-ECG CNN for ALVD screening (EF≤35%) with AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7% on 52,870 patients, and a 4.1× future-dysfunction hazard ratio.

**Rejected from Researcher B:** Their original proposal lacked a second paper; the present version correctly uses PCLR + Paper C, but I qualify their claim that a linear classifier on frozen PCLR embeddings can match Paper C's CNN—this requires empirical testing of whether PCLR's pre-training objective preserves subtle contractile-dysfunction features.

**Qualified from Researcher C:** I adopt their methodological principle—contrastive learning as a label-efficiency tool—but reject the bacterial-epithelial domain as irrelevant to ECG-AI. Their emphasis on causal operability, not topical overlap, is retained.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM

PCLR's contrastive objective maximizes agreement between different ECG views of the same patient while minimizing agreement across patients, forcing the encoder to capture inter-patient morphological variation. Paper C's CNN learned ALVD-discriminative features from raw waveforms under full supervision. The causal bridge: freeze PCLR's encoder and fine-tune a shallow classifier on its embeddings using ≤4,500 paired ECG-echo examples. This tests whether PCLR's self-supervised representations are sufficient for ALVD discrimination, or whether Paper C's supervised features encode contractile-dysfunction information not captured by contrastive pre-training.

RESEARCH DESIGN

**Hypothesis:** PCLR embeddings fine-tuned on ≤4,500 labeled ECGs achieve non-inferior ALVD screening AUC (margin 0.03) to Paper C's CNN on an external site.

**Method:** Pre-train PCLR on 3.2M ECGs. Extract embeddings for Site 1 (10,000 paired ECG-echo) and Site 2 (3,000 paired). Fine-tune a two-layer MLP on 4,500 Site-1 embeddings (EF≤35% vs >35%). Compare against Paper C's CNN retrained on identical 4,500 raw ECGs.

**Validation:** Primary: AUC on Site 2. Secondary: sensitivity/specificity at Paper C's operating point; calibration slope; subgroup AUC by age, sex, QRS duration; hazard ratio for future ALVD in initially negative patients. Bootstrap 1,000 resamples for CIs.

WORKING ABSTRACT

We propose testing whether PCLR's contrastive ECG embeddings can replace Paper C's supervised CNN front-end for ALVD screening. Fine-tuning a shallow classifier on 4,500 labeled examples, we assess non-inferior external AUC and preservation of future-risk prediction. This isolates whether self-supervised representations capture contractile-dysfunction features, addressing label scarcity and external validity beyond either paper alone.

FINAL IDEA: PCLR's contrastive ECG embeddings, fine-tuned with ≤4,500 labeled examples, can achieve non-inferior external ALVD screening AUC to Paper C's fully supervised CNN while preserving future-risk hazard prediction.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper C: An AI-enabled ECG convolutional neural network (CNN) screens for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD), defined as ejection fraction ≤35%, with AUC 0.93 and 85.7% accuracy on 52,870 patients. It also predicts future ALVD risk (HR 4.1).

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use the ECG-AI model from Paper C as a low-cost, noninvasive surrogate for cardiac contractile dysfunction. Apply it to a cohort with a second, currently unavailable paper’s contribution—e.g., a wearable continuous ECG patch or a digital health adherence intervention (not provided). The causal link: if the AI-ECG can detect ALVD from single 12-lead snapshots, its output can trigger or guide a second intervention (e.g., medication titration, remote monitoring) whose effect is measured by changes in AI-ECG risk score over time.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Propose a randomized trial in asymptomatic primary-care patients (n≈2,000) with an AI-ECG positive screen but normal echocardiogram. Arm A receives standard care; Arm B receives a nurse-led protocol using serial AI-ECG scores to intensify lifestyle/pharmacologic management. Primary outcome: 12-month change in AI-ECG probability of ALVD. Secondary outcomes: incident echocardiographic ALVD, adherence, and cost. Validation: compare AI-ECG score trajectory against echocardiographic ejection fraction in a 20% subsample at 6 and 12 months.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose integrating an AI-enabled ECG screening tool with a primary-care management pathway to prevent progression from asymptomatic to symptomatic left ventricular dysfunction. Using the validated convolutional neural network from Paper C, we will identify high-risk individuals and test whether serial AI-ECG monitoring plus nurse-led intervention reduces 12-month AI-ECG risk scores and incident echocardiographic dysfunction compared to usual care. This extends Paper C from a single-time screening tool to a longitudinal monitoring and intervention trigger, potentially enabling scalable prevention of heart failure.

FINAL IDEA: Use an AI-ECG model for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction not just to screen once, but as a longitudinal monitoring tool whose serial risk scores drive and evaluate a primary-care intervention to prevent progression to symptomatic heart failure.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper A contributes a mechanistic account of how local environmental cues (e.g., nutrient gradients) modulate bacterial collective motility via quorum-sensing signal diffusion.
- Paper B contributes a quantitative framework for mapping epithelial tissue stress fields from cell-shape anisotropy and junctional tension, validated in wound-healing assays.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Rather than topical overlap, the connection is operational: bacterial quorum-sensing signal concentration can be treated as a diffusible morphogen-like field whose spatial gradient imposes a mechanical stress analog on a substrate. Paper A provides the signal-production/diffusion dynamics; Paper B provides the stress-inference algorithm. The causal bridge is that local signal concentration alters bacterial adhesion or matrix remodeling, generating measurable epithelial-equivalent stress patterns that Paper B’s method can reconstruct from cell geometry.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
- Build a co-culture: epithelial monolayer (from Paper B) overlaid with engineered bacteria (from Paper A) whose quorum-sensing output drives expression of a matrix-remodeling enzyme.
- Measure bacterial signal concentration via fluorescent reporter; measure epithelial cell-shape anisotropy and junctional tension using Paper B’s pipeline.
- Test: does the bacterial signal gradient predict the inferred epithelial stress field? Validate by comparing inferred stress to traction-force microscopy.
- Control: quorum-sensing knockout bacteria; expect no stress-field alignment.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose a cross-kingdom mechano-chemical feedback study. Bacterial quorum-sensing gradients are treated as diffusible cues that remodel epithelial substrate mechanics. By combining bacterial signal-diffusion dynamics with an epithelial stress-inference algorithm, we test whether microbial chemical fields encode mechanical information readable from host cell geometry. This would establish a new causal link between prokaryotic signaling and eukaryotic tissue mechanics, beyond either paper’s scope.

FINAL IDEA: Bacterial quorum-sensing gradients act as diffusible mechanical inputs that can be decoded from epithelial cell-shape stress fields, linking microbial signaling to host tissue mechanics.

The adopted contrastive principle becomes a measurement tool, not a topical link. In the co-culture system, epithelial stress fields (Paper B output) are high-dimensional and sparsely labeled; bacterial quorum-sensing gradients (Paper A output) provide a continuous, self-organizing supervisory signal. I propose using contrastive learning to align epithelial cell-shape embeddings with bacterial signal-gradient embeddings, forcing the model to learn a shared latent space where chemical gradients predict mechanical stress patterns. The causal connection: bacterial signal diffusion alters matrix remodeling, which changes epithelial geometry; contrastive alignment makes that causal relation learnable from paired but unlabeled image fields.

- Co-culture engineered bacteria (Paper A) with epithelial monolayer (Paper B); image bacterial signal via fluorescent reporter and epithelial geometry via membrane label.
- Pre-train a contrastive encoder on paired patches: positive pairs = same spatiotemporal location across modalities; negative pairs = shuffled locations or quorum-sensing knockout controls.
- Fine-tune with sparse traction-force microscopy labels (≤5,000 patches) to predict stress from signal gradients.
- Validation: held-out wound-healing assays; compare inferred stress to traction-force ground truth; test generalization to a chemically perturbed quorum-sensing mutant not seen in training.

Bacterial quorum-sensing gradients and epithelial stress fields are aligned in a shared latent space via self-supervised contrastive learning, using sparse traction-force labels for fine-tuning. This tests whether microbial chemical fields encode mechanical information decodable from host cell geometry, and whether contrastive pre-training reduces labeled-data needs in mechanobiology. The contribution beyond either paper is a new causal-measurement bridge between prokaryotic signaling and eukaryotic tissue mechanics.
